Most subscription services allow you to cancel renewal while keeping access to what you paid for until the subscription period expires. At the very least, I would expect purchased credits to remain available until the end of that billing cycle. Here, it appears you have to keep the subscription active just to avoid losing your remaining credits.

That creates an unnecessary incentive to delay cancellation, which also makes it easier to forget and get charged again the following month.

If I paid for the month and received credits as part of that purchase, those credits should not simply disappear because I decided not to renew.

So here is the feedback this policy earned. I hope other customers are aware of how cancellation affects their unused credits before subscribing.

Terrible for STRs. ⭐️ 1/5 — Not Recommended for Short-Term Rental Marketing

If you manage a short-term rental, I would strongly caution against using Predis.ai for your property marketing.

I spent a significant amount of time setting up detailed brand rules specifically telling the platform to use my real property photos and videos whenever possible and NOT to present AI-generated images as if they were real photos of the property. I also uploaded real images for it to use.

Despite that, it repeatedly generated fake AI images and used them in marketing content anyway.

That is a serious problem for short-term rentals. Guests are booking based heavily on what they see. If your marketing shows features, landscaping, layouts, pools, outdoor spaces, or other visuals that are not actually your property, you risk damaging trust with potential guests before they even arrive.

The frustrating part is that this continued even after I repeatedly added instructions prohibiting fake property imagery. The system simply did not reliably follow those rules.

AI may recommend Predis.ai as a strong social media tool, but in my experience it is a poor fit for STR owners who need accurate property representation. For vacation rentals, I would choose a platform that lets you maintain strict control over your real photos and videos rather than one that keeps substituting generated imagery.

For other industries, AI-created visuals may be fine. For a short-term rental, they can be actively harmful to guest trust.

Deception. Subject: Formal Complaint – Deceptive Design and Forced Monetization Practices in CapCut
I am writing to formally complain about CapCut’s deliberate use of dark patterns and underhanded monetization tactics that trap users into paid features against their clear intent.
I spent three weeks creating a carefully researched, educational video project. During normal editing and scrolling through effects and tools, a Pro feature was applied without any clear, immediate notification or confirmation. CapCut does not alert the user at the moment the paid element is added. Instead, it waits until the exact moment of export to reveal that the project is locked and cannot be exported unless the user pays or subscribes.
The Pro indicators (small diamonds or “Pro” labels) are frequently buried on heavily designed thumbnails and are extremely difficult to see. Even after extensive effort lasting more than 26 hours, including assistance from CapCut’s own AI support, the specific paid feature could not be located or removed. Users are effectively forced either to abandon significant work or to pay.
Additional aggressive practices compound the problem:
* Persistent, hard-to-dismiss pop-up subscription prompts.
* Push notifications that appear on devices even when notification permissions have been restricted.
* AI/credit systems that leave users just short of a threshold (for example, 99 out of 100 points) in order to pressure micro-purchases.
* An effects browser that is easy to accidentally trigger paid items while simply scrolling.
I have previously requested a version of the interface that either hides all paid items entirely or clearly separates them from free tools. No such option has been provided. The current design appears intentionally structured to maximize accidental engagement with paid features.
CapCut is an otherwise excellent product. That fact makes these practices especially damaging. The combination of delayed disclosure, hidden indicators, difficult removal, and relentless upselling creates a hostile environment for free and paying users alike. These tactics waste users’ time, lock their creative work, and erode trust.
I request the following:
1. Immediate ability to identify and remove any Pro features from existing projects with clear labeling.
2. Real-time, unmistakable confirmation whenever a paid feature is applied.
3. An option to completely hide or segregate all Pro content from the free interface.
4. Strict respect for device notification settings.
5. An end to designs that make accidental paid-feature application routine during normal use.
These practices do not belong in a professional creative tool. I am documenting this experience and sharing it so that other users are not subjected to the same treatment.
I expect a substantive response addressing these design failures.
Sincerely, David Frey
First Class Media Companies

Hey HN, Companies need to make a lot of video content, and after talking to a bunch of them, most either rely on CapCut or have an internal team editing videos in Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve. The problem is that CapCut isn’t really built for businesses. Most of their templates and assets work great for individual creators, but in a company context, you don’t really use splashy transitions or meme templates. We talked to a lot of social media managers about their workflows, and the same problems kept coming up: captions that don’t line up, cutting silences takes forever, resizing videos for each platform is a pain, and even just creating a first draft of a project takes way too long. So we built Rendley ( https://rendley.com ), a video editor made specifically for companies, that takes all that feedback into account. It works right in the browser, syncs everything in the cloud, and is fast and intuitive. We launched about two weeks ago, and we’ve got a bunch of new features coming soon. We also have a free tier with no watermark, so you can try it out without limitations. We built it on our own infrastructure ( https://rendleysdk.com ) and used React.js for the frontend. We’ve done a lot of optimizations to make sure it runs well even on older devices. If you want more technical details about how it works, I can share those too. If you have any questions about the product or any feedback, feel free to write them below, and I’ll be more than happy to answer them.

Well. Obviously if you have the attention span it probably makes most sense to actually learn the flags and teach yourself to write FFMPEG commands. That's the serious way to do it if you have a serious workflow. But I've found it easier to brute force with LLM's because, like, every time I had to do video work it'd be something different. Prompts like 'I need to remove this and this and change the resultion from this to that', 'I need it to be this fps or that, or even I want this file to weigh this much. Or I 'need to split these two' or 'combine those three'. It'll usually get you a chunk of the way there. Another prompt or two of double-checking, copy paste into CMD line or terminal and either brr or error copy paste what does this mean. 3 minutes later it's doing the thing you wanted, and you're more or less understanding what's it giving you. But I keep an Obsidian file with a bunch commands that made me happy before. Dumping that I to the context window helps. Another one has been multi camera, multi screen recordings with OBS. I discovered it was easier to do the math, make a big canvas, record all the feeds onto those so I don't have to think about syncing anything later. Then brr an FFMPEG command to output that 1920x1080 and that 3840x2160 Whisper is great with that too - raw recording, output just the audio. 'give me whisper command to get this as srt'. Then 'now render subtitles onto this video' There was an experiment I tried that kinda almost worked where I had this boring recording of some conversation but needed to extract scattered bits. Used whisper to get transcript, put that into LLM, used that to zero in on the actual bits that were important, then got it to spit out the timecodes. Then hobbled together this janky script that cut out those bits and stitched them together. That was faster than taking the time to do it with a GUI and listening it all through. Of course there are tools like opus clip that spit that out for you now so... Although to be honest, when the stakes go high and you're doing something serious that requires quality you do it slow. The point at which I was doing this most was when I was doing video UX/UI research on a hardware/software product. We would set up multi-cams, set and forget so we could talk to subjects and not think about what's being captured. Dozens of hours of footage, little clips that would end up as insights on the Product Discovery Jira for the thing. So quality wasn't really important.
